analysis.one_liner: Requires portable generators to meet carbon monoxide safety standards including automatic shutoff.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a Democrat and one Republican, never received a hearing or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Every year, people are poisoned by carbon monoxide from portable generators, most often during power outages when a generator is run too close to a home or its exhaust drifts indoors. This bill ordered the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write a binding safety standard within a year, requiring carbon monoxide concentration limits, clear exhaust-direction labels, a power cord at least 30 feet long, and a generator that shuts itself off when carbon monoxide builds up. It also banned the sale of generators that do not already meet two existing industry safety standards, with an interim shutoff requirement, starting six months after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Families who own or borrow portable generators during storms and outages, the group that suffers most carbon monoxide poisoning deaths and brain injuries from this product.

how_it_helps.text: Orders the CPSC to issue a final safety standard within one year, incorporating carbon monoxide concentration limits from the ANSI/UL 2201 and ANSI/PGMA G300 standards, clear exhaust-direction labeling, a 30-foot minimum power cord, and automatic shutoff in elevated carbon monoxide conditions [S2] [S3].

Starting six months after enactment, bans importing or selling portable generators that do not meet ANSI/UL 2201 or ANSI/PGMA G300-2018 and that lack an engine shutoff before carbon monoxide exceeds 600 ppm or a 10-minute average of 275 ppm [S3].
Requires the CPSC to review and revise the standard at least every five years and authorizes enforcement against violations [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Portable generator manufacturers, who would have to redesign engines with carbon monoxide shutoff sensors and lower emission rates, update labeling, and supply longer cords; some of that cost would likely reach buyers as higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for redesigning engines and adding shutoff sensors would likely raise generator prices, which fall hardest on lower-income households that buy them precisely because they cannot afford better backup power [S3].

The bill ties the standard to specific existing industry standards (ANSI/UL 2201 and ANSI/PGMA G300-2018), which could lock in those private benchmarks as the legal floor and require regulation to update them as successors [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gain is large and targeted: portable generators are a leading cause of carbon monoxide poisoning deaths during power outages, and automatic shutoff directly addresses that. The cost is higher purchase prices and redesign work for manufacturers, a trade-off typical of product safety rules. The interim six-month requirement was relatively quick for companies already selling to stricter standards, so the design is reasonable rather than badly flawed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2021, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Health Subcommittee, and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush (D-IL) introduced the bill on December 2, 2021, joined by Rep. Duncan, making it bipartisan at introduction [S1] [S3] [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and three days later to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Portable generator manufacturers avoided a federal mandate to add carbon monoxide shutoff capability and meet tighter emission limits, and buyers avoided price increases that redesign would have caused, while the risk of poisoning deaths from cheaper generators remained unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Generator makers avoided new safety mandates

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan at introduction, a Democrat and one Republican cosponsor, and the bill drew no recorded opposition; it died from inaction rather than a partisan vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required redesigned engines with automatic carbon monoxide shutoff, lower emission rates, longer cords, and warning labels, imposing redesign and compliance costs. The same design changes are what prevent the poisoning deaths the bill targets, so the industry's interest in avoiding them runs against consumer safety.

The bill would have given the Consumer Product Safety Commission a mandatory deadline and enforcement authority over portable generators, strengthening its hand against industry resistance. The agency's interest in a safety mandate runs with consumers'.
